This bracelet design is one involving 8 pieces
formed into an octagon then turned to style.
First off, a thank you to the FVWG member
Jim Peardon who first introduced me to the
idea some years ago when Gerry Vickers and
I visited their Guild meeting. The next stage
came after the sketch had been shuffled
around on my workbench for two or three
years. This part is worth telling as it illustrates
one of the great things about woodturning
and that is the friendship and camaraderie
that the results from being involved. I had a
friend who had been fighting cancer for several years. About two and a half years ago,
after a few visits to my shop, he decided it
would be nice to turn a bowl for the nurses
where he took his chemo. He was pleased
with his results and then filled the bowl with
candies on his visits. One day he noticed the
bracelet plans on the bench and asked if that
was something he could do for his wife and
two daughters. Well, many measurements
and two prototypes later, the three bracelets
were done. Although Bruce is gone, his girls
will enjoy his work for a long time. It gives
me a warm feeling each time I think of Bruce.
Now the making of the bracelet.
1. Preparing stock: There are many combinations, but I will describe the four wood
version. You need 4 pieces of contrasting
wood. Maple, walnut, cherry and purple
heart are used here. Dimensions are 8“ x
1.5” x .625-.75” with attention to how the
nice grain will show. Cut two pieces of
each with the long side at 1.75” and both
ends at 45 degrees.
2. Dry assembly: Place the pieces together
to shape the octagon then pencil mark the
joints.
3. Glue up: I use epoxy as it does better for
me if there are oily woods involved. First

Once the material is securely held, the
turning can begin. In some ways, it is
easier than turning wood. Since metal
has no fibers you can turn uphill or
downhill, and there is less chance of
getting a catch. However, use caution
and do not try to grab shavings that
are wrapped around the spindle as you
will cut yourself. Similarly, be careful
not to leave sharp edges.
Normal grits of sandpaper can be used
to sand the piece, but be aware that a
black gunge may build up. This gunge
can be removed by using Sunlight dishwashing liquid on an abrasive pad.
Beeswax makes a nice finish.
As usual, it was a carefully thought out
and well presented demonstration.
Thanks Bruce!
Despite being plagued by a cold, Bruce
showed us how to turn an aluminum
finial on a regular wood lathe. Much
of the process looked familiar: most
of the usual tools can be used without
any modification. There is no need to
change the grind on the gouges, skews
or the parting tools necessary for the
project. It is, however, necessary to
sharpen more often.
Finial material is available from basic
hardware stores like Home Depot and
Rona. Copper, brass and aluminum all
turn well. Bronze is too hard, and you
will have to sharpen your tools too
often.
The first problem that arises in turning
metal is how do you hold the stock?
The best solution is a collet chuck or
spigot jaws. In order to minimize
chatter, Bruce feeds the material in
through the outboard end of the headstock, through the hollow spindle and
into the chuck. As a result, he can

I’m thrifty. I’m also in an enviable position in that I work at VGH and see all
sorts of good stuff that is destined for
the recycling bin. I am also a firm believer that part of recycling is finding
another use for stuff that is of no use
for its original purpose. All machines
are just made up of sub systems of
things that can be put together a different way to suit a new purpose. I guess
you could also say that I like to tinker.
If I can find something that is going to
make my life in my shop a bit better
then I’m all for that.
I had for some time been on the look
out for a way of improving my dust collection system for my lathe. I had made
it a priority to replace my entire dust
collection system in my shop to try and
get a handle on the mess. Last summer
I installed a new Oneida 2HP Super
Gorilla cyclone dust collector. This
involved redesigning all the ductwork
with spiral metal ducts, new blast gates
and pickup points for the dust. Of
course I wanted to incorporate some
old medical equipment
to personalize the new
system.
I’m sure that many of
you have had the experience of having some xrays taken of you some
time in your life. In an
x-ray suite the system of
x-y movement of some
of the apparatus attached to the ceiling is
known as a gantry. I had
been on the lookout for
one for some time now.
I didn’t really need the
entire x-y unit and was
being particular as to
what I wanted to obtain.

they have a smaller gantry that is just one axis
of movement that is

Sandpaper clips and Velcro strips
Dennis Cloutier
After seeing Larry’s shop, his method
of holding sandpaper inspired me to
get some sticky-backed Velcro loop
tape and put it up near both lathes. I
wrote the grits directly on the loop
tape. I also got some magnetic belt
clips from Lee Valley to hold regular
cloth-backed sandpaper, and wrote the
grit numbers on the clips. These get
stuck on the headstock of one lathe,
and on the dust collection duct by the
other lathe. My way isn’t as, um…
frugal, as Larry’s, but it was less work.
Sandpaper Easel
Larry Stevenson
I needed some way of organizing my
sandpaper for use at my lathe and
came up with the following system.
Nothing fancy, however it works for
me: a piece of plywood with one side
having many clothespins glued to it
with the number for the appropriate
grit of paper. The other side has Velcro hook on it so that I can stick all
my Velcro paper on it. On the bottom is some recycled medical equipment, a horseshoe magnet from a galvanometer out of some old piece of
equipment that was destined for the

Bonnie Klein Biography
Bonnie has been seriously involved
with woodturning since the early
1980’s. In 1986 she designed the small
Klein Lathe which has been in production for over 20 years. In 1992 she
introduced the Threading Jig as an
accessory to the lathe for cutting
threads in wood. Bonnie has produced 5 turning videos which have
now been converted to DVD’s and in
2005 wrote a woodturning project
book. She has demonstrated and
taught workshops in many countries as
well as all over the USA. In 2003 she
was made an AAW Honorary Lifetime
Member in recognition of her contributions to woodturning.
Martin P. Thorne Biography
Martin has been making objects since
childhood. His first turning experience
was in his father’s workshop: the
lathe, a “Wolf” electric drill; the tailstock, a block of wood and a sharpened screw; the cutting tool, a boxwood handled Marples paring chisel.
That was fifty years ago and his lifelong
passion for making fine objects continues unabated – his favorite tool, the
lathe!
Today Martin’s work is influenced by
his surroundings, the Squamish Estuary, Howe Sound, and the mountains.
He uses local materials, recycled,
found on the beaches or rivers, or
salvaged from the logging industry.
Martin has owned and operated a custom woodworking studio in Squamish,
BC for thirty years. His work can be
found in private collections worldwide

Sandpaper Roll Organizer:
Bruce Campbell
The annual AAW Symposium is coming up in Portland, OR (June 29 – July
1). The last time the AAW Symposium was this close to us was in 1999
in Tacoma, WA. (where we received
our AAW chapter designation) and I
expect it will be some while before it
returns. These, plus the fact that it is
always a terrific event, are excellent
reasons to attend. Go on-line at
http://www.woodturner.org for more
information.
Things are beginning to pick up for our
Symposium in September. Please think
about what you would like to do to
help out and either approach that
team leader or contact Steve Kent,
Volunteer Coordinator, who will help
get you involved.
Finally, just a reminder to bring in your
Easter Eggs for the President’s Challenge. Then, start working on Larry’s
nasty challenge for May. Turn a plug
exactly 1” in diameter and 1” long.
Then turn a hole in another piece also
exactly 1” in diameter and 1” deep. Fit
them together and bring them to the
challenge in May. The fun will be to
see if all the pegs can be interchanged
and still fit.
Our last meeting was very well attended (over 80 people) and I want to
thank Lance Rossington for his delightful step-by-step demonstration for
turning an eight-piece bracelet.
Thanks, also, to Larry Stevenson, our
new vice-president, for stepping in to
chair the meeting while I showed some
of what I have learned about turning
soft metals in the same way we turn
wood. I hope it was not too boring.
I was delighted to announce at the
meeting that the Board has created a
very special award called the Outstanding Contribution Award. This
award is intended to recognize contributions to the Guild that have shaped
(or reshaped) it in a significant way.
As a result, the Board expects that the
award will not be presented very often. Nevertheless, any Guild member
many be nominated by five or more
members (the nomination form is
available on our web site). The completed form should be forwarded to
the Secretary of the Guild who will
present it to the next Board meeting
for consideration. If the Board approves the nomination the member
will receive the award at an appropriate time chosen by the Board. Please
have a look at the guidelines for this
award on http://www.gvwg.ca

2008 call for artists for Exhibit at Place
des Arts, Maillardville, Coquitlam
Place des Arts is currently accepting proposals for its 2008 exhibitions. They offer
gallery and gift shop display space where
local, emerging artists and artisans may exhibit and sell their works in any media.
They are located at 1120 Brunette Avenue,
Coquitlam. The galleries are open to the
public 7 days a week and are a popular destination with local residents and visitors
alike: in 2005, they had 63,428 visits. They
welcome submissions in all 2D and 3D media and techniques. Details and an application form can be found on their website at
www.placedesarts.ca. Proposals will be accepted until June 1, 2007. Phone 604-6641636 for more information.
